source: It was a Saturday night, and such a Sabbath as followed! Ex officio professors of Sabbath breaking are all whalemen. The ivory Pequod was turned into what seemed a shamble; every sailor a butcher. You would have thought we were offering up ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods.

In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles, among other ponderous things comprising a cluster of blocks generally painted green, and which no single man can possibly lift—this vast bunch of grapes was swayed up to the main-top and firmly lashed to the lower mast-head, the strongest point anywhere above a ship’s deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies, was then conducted to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now suspended in stages over the side, Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook just above the nearest of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut round the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew striking up a wild chorus, now commence heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. When instantly, the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frighted mast-heads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the billows; till at last, a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upwards and backwards from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight dragging after it the disengaged semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now as the blubber envelopes the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so is it stripped off from the body precisely as an orange is sometimes stripped by spiralizing it. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass continually keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and as the blubber in one strip uniformly peels off along the line called the “scarf,” simultaneously cut by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is thus peeled off, and indeed by that very act itself, it is all the time being hoisted higher and higher aloft till its upper end grazes the main-top; the men at the windlass then cease heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and every one present must take good heed to dodge it when it swings, else it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

One of the attending harpooneers now advances with a long, keen weapon called a boarding-sword, and watching his chance he dexterously slices out a considerable hole in the lower part of the swaying mass. Into this hole, the end of the second alternating great tackle is then hooked so as to retain a hold upon the blubber, in order to prepare for what follows. Whereupon, this accomplished swordsman, warning all hands to stand off, once more makes a scientific dash at the mass, and with a few sidelong, desperate, lunging slicings, severs it completely in twain; so that while the short lower part is still fast, the long upper strip, called a blanket-piece, swings clear, and is all ready for lowering. The heavers forward now resume their song, and while the one tackle is peeling and hoisting a second strip from the whale, the other is slowly slackened away, and down goes the first strip through the main hatchway right beneath, into an unfurnished parlor called the blubber-room. Into this twilight apartment sundry nimble hands keep coiling away the long blanket-piece as if it were a great live mass of plaited serpents. And thus the work proceeds; the two tackles hoisting and lowering simultaneously; both whale and windlass heaving, the heavers singing, the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and all hands swearing occasionally, by way of assuaging the general friction.

modern_en.title: Chapter 67 — Cutting In
paragraphs: It was a Saturday night, and such a Sabbath as followed! By their very profession, all whalemen are breakers of the Sabbath. The ivory Pequod was turned into what seemed a slaughterhouse. Every sailor was a butcher. You would have thought we were sacrificing ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods.

In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles were hoisted up to the main-top. Among other ponderous things, they include a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift; and this vast bunch of grapes was firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended over the side on stages (planks slung from the ship as platforms), Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

One of the harpooners standing by now steps forward with a long, sharp weapon called a boarding-sword, waits for his moment, and deftly cuts a sizable hole in the lower part of the swinging mass. The end of the second of the two great alternating tackles is then hooked into this hole to keep a grip on the blubber and prepare for what comes next. Then this accomplished swordsman warns everyone to stand clear, makes one more scientific lunge at the mass, and with a few desperate, sidelong, slashing strokes cuts it clean in two. The short lower part stays fast, while the long upper strip, called a blanket-piece, swings free, ready to be lowered. The heavers forward now strike up their song again. While one tackle peels and hoists a second strip off the whale, the other is slowly eased off, and down goes the first strip through the main hatchway directly below, into a bare parlor called the blubber-room. In this twilight room a number of nimble hands keep coiling away the long blanket-piece as though it were a great living heap of braided snakes. And so the work goes on: the two tackles hoisting and lowering together; whale and windlass both heaving, the heavers singing, the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and everyone swearing now and then to ease the general friction.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 67 — Flænsningen
paragraphs: Det var en lørdag aften, og sikken en sabbat der fulgte! Af selve deres erhverv er alle hvalfangere sabbatsbrydere. Det elfenbenshvide Pequod blev forvandlet til noget, der lignede et slagteri. Hver sømand var en slagter. Man skulle have troet, at vi ofrede ti tusind røde okser til havguderne.

For det første blev de enorme skæretakler hejst op til stortoppen. Blandt andre tunge ting indeholder de en klynge af blokke, der som regel er malet grønne, og som ikke en enkelt mand kan løfte. Denne store drueklase blev surret fast til underste mastetop, det stærkeste punkt overhovedet over et skibs dæk. Enden af det tovværk, der er tykt som en trosse, og som snor sig gennem disse indviklede dele, blev så ført til ankerspillet, og den svære nederste blok i taklerne blev svunget ud over hvalen. I denne blok blev den store spækkrog fastgjort, som vejer omkring hundrede pund. Og nu, hængende ud over siden på platforme (planker hængt ud fra skibet som standpladser), begyndte Starbuck og Stubb, styrmændene, bevæbnet med deres lange spader, at skære et hul i kroppen til at sætte krogen i, lige over den nærmeste af de to sidefinner. Når det er gjort, skæres en bred, halvcirkelformet linje rundt om hullet, krogen sættes i, og hovedparten af mandskabet, der slår op med et vildt omkvæd, begynder nu at hive i én tæt klump ved ankerspillet. Straks krænger hele skibet over på siden. Hver eneste bolt i det rykker sig som sømhovederne i et gammelt hus i frostvejr. Det dirrer, ryster og nikker sine forskrækkede mastetoppe mod himlen. Mere og mere læner det sig ind mod hvalen, mens hvert gispende hiv i ankerspillet besvares af et hjælpende hiv fra bølgerne, indtil man til sidst hører et hurtigt, forskrækkende smæld. Med et stort plask ruller skibet opad og baglæns væk fra hvalen, og det sejrende takkel kommer til syne og trækker den løsnede, halvcirkelformede ende af den første strimmel spæk efter sig. Nu, da spækket omslutter hvalen netop som skrællen en appelsin, bliver det trukket af kroppen netop som en appelsin nogle gange skrælles — i en spiral. For den spænding, som ankerspillet hele tiden holder oppe, får hvalen til at rulle rundt og rundt i vandet, og spækket skrælles af i én jævn strimmel langs linjen, der kaldes »skråsnittet«, som samtidig skæres af Starbucks og Stubbs spader, styrmændenes. Og lige så hurtigt som det skrælles af, og faktisk netop ved selve den handling, hejses det højere og højere op, indtil dets øverste ende strejfer stortoppen. Mændene ved ankerspillet holder så op med at hive, og et øjeblik eller to svinger den enorme, blodtriflende masse frem og tilbage, som om den var firet ned fra himlen. Og enhver tilstedeværende må passe godt på at vige for den, når den svinger, ellers kan den give ham en lussing og kaste ham på hovedet over bord.

En af harpunererne, der står parat, træder nu frem med et langt, skarpt redskab, som kaldes et entresværd, venter på det rette øjeblik og skærer behændigt et stort hul i den nederste del af den svingende masse. Enden af det andet af de to store skiftevis virkende taljer hager man så fast i hullet, så man kan holde fast i spækket og gøre klar til det, der kommer. Derefter råber den dygtige sværdmand, at alle skal holde sig fri, støder endnu en gang videnskabeligt mod massen og skærer den med nogle desperate, skråtgående hug helt over i to dele. Den korte nederste del bliver siddende, mens den lange øverste strimmel, som kaldes et tæppestykke, svinger frit, klar til at blive firet ned. Hejserne forude tager nu deres sang op igen. Mens den ene talje flår og hejser en ny strimmel af hvalen, firer man langsomt den anden, og den første strimmel går ned gennem det store lugehul lige nedenunder, ind i en nøgen stue, der kaldes spækrummet. I dette halvmørke rum er en række adrætte hænder hele tiden i gang med at lægge det lange tæppestykke sammen i ringe, som var det en stor levende bunke flettede slanger. Og sådan går arbejdet videre: De to taljer hejser og fire på samme tid, hval og ankerspil trækker begge to, hejserne synger, herrerne i spækrummet lægger i ringe, styrmændene skærer til, skibet knager, og alle bander en gang imellem for at tage skraldet af den almindelige gnidning.
